extracted.intended_audience: inventors and patent applicants (including independent inventors, small businesses) and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on U.S. patentability standards and the procedural, formal, and substantive requirements for preparing, filing, and prosecuting patent applications (utility, design, and plant) at the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is a patent / rights conferred
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is the grant of a property right to the inventor issued by the USPTO; generally the term of a new patent is 20 years from the filing date (subject to maintenance fees), and the grant confers 'the right to exclude others from making, using, offering for sale, or selling' the invention in the United States or importing the invention into the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent grants are effective only in the U.S., U.S. territories, and possessions; patent term extensions/adjustments may be available; the patent confers an exclusionary right (not a right to make/use) and the patentee must enforce rights independently of the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Three types of patents exist: (1) Utility patents for new and useful processes, machines, manufactures, compositions of matter, or improvements; (2) Design patents for new, original, and ornamental designs for articles of manufacture; (3) Plant patents for distinct and new varieties of asexually reproduced plants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each patent type has specific subject-matter scope and some procedural differences (e.g., design/plant have single-claim conventions, plant patents require botanical description and certain drawing/color rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter (statutory classes and exclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter: any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof; however, courts have held laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent law's statutory categories are broad (include industrial/technical processes, manufactured articles, chemical compositions), but novelty/non-obviousness/usefulness and judicial exceptions limit eligibility; a mere idea/suggestion is not patentable — a complete description of the actual subject matter is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility / Usefulness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter must be 'useful' — meaning it has a useful purpose and is operative; a machine that will not operate to perform the intended purpose is not 'useful' and is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operativeness is required; the specification should demonstrate the invention's practical utility where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (anticipation) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is not patentable if, before its effective filing date, the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public, or described in a U.S. patent or published patent application naming another inventor filed earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Otherwise available to the public’ includes oral presentations, demonstrations, trade shows, radio, YouTube, websites, and other online material. There are limited exceptions (see one-year inventor disclosure grace period below).

rubrics_metrics.name: One-year inventor disclosure exception (grace period)
rubrics_metrics.description: An exception may apply to a 'disclosure made 1 year or less before the effective filing date' if the disclosure was made by the inventor/joint inventor or by someone who obtained the subject matter from the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a limited exception to the statutory bars; public disclosures by others generally start the clock against patentability unless they derive from the inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective filing date / priority basics
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'effective filing date' for a U.S. nonprovisional application is the actual filing date of the nonprovisional; it can be the filing date of an earlier U.S. provisional (if the provisional sufficiently describes the claimed invention), an earlier-filed U.S. nonprovisional (continuation/division), or an earlier foreign application to which priority is claimed (if that foreign application sufficiently describes the claimed invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properly supported priority claims can provide earlier effective dates for novelty and obviousness determinations; adequacy of the earlier application's description is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obviousness (inventive step) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if differences exist over known art, an invention may be refused if those differences would be obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the relevant technology; routine substitutions (e.g., color changes, size changes) are ordinarily not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment is factual and depends on the knowledge of a PHOSITA; the specification and claim drafting should emphasize non-routine advantages and inventive features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application components for a nonprovisional patent application
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonprovisional application includes: (1) A written document comprising a specification (description and claims); (2) Drawings (when necessary); (3) An oath or declaration; and (4) Filing, search, and examination fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All required parts must comply with rules to obtain a filing date; missing parts may generate a Notice of Incomplete Application and possibly a surcharge; filing fee and declaration need not be submitted to get a filing date but omitting them may trigger notices and deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and claims: required content and role
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification (description and claims) must particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter the applicant regards as the invention; the claims define the scope of protection. The specification must conclude with a claim or claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must commence on a separate sheet; multiple claims are permitted provided they differ; dependent claims may refer back and further limit other claims; multiple dependent claims are allowed and have special treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal formatting requirements for application papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Each document must have margins: top ≥ 2 cm (3/4 inch), left ≥ 2.5 cm (1 inch), right ≥ 2 cm (3/4 inch), bottom ≥ 2 cm (3/4 inch); no holes; spacing should be 1.5 or double; pages must be numbered consecutively starting with page one; single column of text; nonscript fonts (e.g., Arial, Times Roman, Courier), preferably 12 pt, with capital letters at least 0.3175 cm (0.125 inch) high but no smaller than 0.21 cm (0.08 inch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formalities apply to documents (preferably filed as PDF via EFS-Web); adherence avoids objections/defects that can delay filing dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing methods and non-electronic filing fee
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective November 15, 2011, any regular nonprovisional utility application filed by mail or hand-delivery requires payment of an additional $400 'non-electronic filing fee' (reduced 50% for qualifying small entities; micro-entity discount does not apply to the fee), unless the regular nonprovisional utility application is filed via EFS-Web.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design, plant, and provisional applications are not subject to the non-electronic filing fee and may be filed by mail/hand-delivery; if you receive a 'Notice of Incomplete Application' after EFS-Web filing, you must become a Registered eFiler and file your reply via EFS-Web to avoid the $400 fee (or pay the fee if filing by mail).

rubrics_metrics.name: EFS-Web Registered eFiler rules for follow-on correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not have to be a Registered eFiler to file a patent application via EFS-Web; however, unregistered eFilers are not permitted to file follow-on correspondence via EFS-Web. Follow-on correspondence filed by anyone other than a Registered eFiler must be sent by mail or hand-delivered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To have the ability to file follow-on correspondence online, become a Registered eFiler; contact the Electronic Business Center for assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All application documents must be in the English language or a translation into English will be required along with the required fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-English documents must be translated and accompanied by the required fee to avoid processing delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page/paper submission and document linking when filing parts separately
rubrics_metrics.description: If parts of the application are not filed together, each part must be signed and accompanied by a letter accurately and clearly connecting it with the other parts of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing all parts together is desirable; otherwise, separate parts may delay obtaining a filing date or trigger notices and surcharges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing fees reductions for small and micro entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees for filing, searching, examining, issuing, appealing, and maintaining patents are reduced by 50% for qualifying small entities under 37 CFR 1.27(a) and by 75% for qualifying micro entities under 37 CFR 1.29(a) or (d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must determine entitlement to small or micro entity status before asserting the status and paying reduced fees; there are specific micro-entity certification forms (PTO/SB/15A and PTO/SB/15B). Fees change each October; filing electronically via EFS-Web can further reduce fees for small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence and addressing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: All business with the USPTO should be transacted in writing. Correspondence concerning an application must include the application number (or serial number and filing date) or the international application number. Correspondence concerning a patent should include patentee name, invention title, patent number, and date of issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate letters should be written for each distinct subject (assignments, payments, orders, responses to Office actions); mail stops should be used when appropriate; include full return addresses. Papers violating decorum/courtesy may be returned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and public availability of applications and patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications that are not published or issued are not generally open to the public and information is released only on written authority of the applicant/assignee/attorney, or when necessary to USPTO business. Patent application publications and patents are published/made available (most applications published 18 months from earliest effective filing date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents, published applications, assignment records (except certain unpublished application assignments), and other records are open to public inspection in the USPTO Search Room or by ordering copies; unpublished applications are kept confidential absent proper authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art searching and Public Search Facility / PTRCs
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors may perform preliminary searches at the USPTO Public Search Facility or Patent and Trademark Resource Centers (PTRCs) and may order copies of patents. PTRCs maintain patent collections and offer assistance and search aids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary searches by inventors may not be as complete as USPTO examiner searches; examiners may reject claims based on prior art not found in preliminary searches. Contact PTRCs for hours/services; use Cassis CD-ROM and other tools available at PTRCs for classification and searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation: patent attorneys and patent agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation and prosecution of a patent application require knowledge of patent law, Office practice, and technical matters. Most inventors employ registered patent attorneys or agents. The USPTO registers both attorneys and non-attorney patent agents (who must meet educational and examination requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registered practitioners prepare applications and conduct prosecution; patent agents cannot practice general law (e.g., drawing contracts) in many jurisdictions. The USPTO maintains a register/directory of registered practitioners and may discipline (disbar/suspend) for misconduct after hearing. USPTO will not recommend particular practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may apply / inventorship rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor or a person to whom the inventor has assigned or is under obligation to assign may apply for a patent. If the inventor is deceased or legally incapacitated, legal representatives may apply. Joint inventors apply as joint inventors; a mere financial contributor is not a joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors in inventorship (omitting or erroneously naming inventors) can be corrected. USPTO officers/employees are prohibited by law from applying for or acquiring patents except by inheritance or bequest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims drafting conventions (independent/dependent/multiple dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be independent (stand alone) or dependent (referring back to and further limiting another claim). A dependent claim that refers back to more than one other claim is a 'multiple dependent claim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims define protection scope; dependent and multiple dependent claims have specific formal and substantive rules — claims must commence on a separate sheet and differ from one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent substantive and formal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents protect only the ornamental appearance of an article of manufacture; the specification is short and follows a set form; only one claim is permitted; drawings define the scope of protection; no reference characters allowed in drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patent term: design patents issuing on/after May 13, 2015 have a 15-year term from grant (previously 14 years). On examination, a notice of allowance triggers payment of an issue fee. See current fee schedule for filing fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant patent substantive and formal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Plant patents cover distinct and new varieties of plants that are asexually reproduced (not tuber-propagated or found in uncultivated state); an application must include a complete detailed botanical description, origin/parentage, how it was asexually reproduced, and the Latin genus/species name. Only one claim is permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If color is distinctive, identify color by a recognized color dictionary and submit color drawings (two duplicate copies). Plant patent drawings must disclose distinctive characteristics; specimens generally should not be submitted unless requested. Plant patents have a 20-year term from filing and cannot be filed via EFS-Web.

rubrics_metrics.name: International protection, treaties, and priority periods
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. patent rights are territorial; to obtain protection abroad, file in each country or region. Paris Convention grants right of priority: subsequent applications based on a first application must be filed within 12 months for patents (6 months for designs/trademarks). The Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) facilitates centralized initial filing and search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing an international (PCT) application affords an international filing date and a centralized search and delays national phase deadlines. For inventions made in the U.S., a license from the Director of the USPTO is required to file abroad before filing in the U.S. or within six months unless earlier license indicated in filing receipt; secrecy orders affect foreign filing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing abroad for foreign applicants and claiming foreign priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign applicants may apply for U.S. patents on the same basis as U.S. citizens, but special points apply: an oath/declaration signature is required; to claim priority to a foreign application, the U.S. application must be filed within 12 months (6 months for designs) of the earlier foreign filing and a certified copy of the foreign application may be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The oath/declaration must identify foreign applications filed more than a year before the U.S. filing that disclose similar inventions; procedures exist for taking oaths before foreign officials and for using declarations instead of oaths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent marking and 'Patent Pending' usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who makes or sells patented articles (or someone doing so for the patentee) is required to mark articles with the word 'patent' and the patent number; failure to mark may preclude recovery of damages unless the infringer had actual notice and continued to infringe after notice. Marking as 'patent applied for' or 'patent pending' has no legal effect but informs the public; false marking is unlawful and subject to penalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate marking is required to preserve certain damages; avoid false or deceptive patent marking statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement enforcement and USPTO jurisdiction limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has no jurisdiction over patent infringement questions; infringement suits are federal court matters; infringement is primarily determined by the language of the claims; defendants may challenge patent validity in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From district court decisions there is appeal to the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit and potentially to the Supreme Court. For U.S. government infringement, remedies lie in the Court of Federal Claims; the USPTO does not advise on infringement or whether an invention infringes existing patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination structure and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO examination work is divided among examining technology centers (TCs) with examiners who review applications and determine entitlement to patents. Appeals from examiner refusals go to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB); petitions and certain reviews may be made to the Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational structure affects who reviews applications and where appeals/petitions are directed; understanding TC jurisdiction aids in prosecution strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public resources, facilities, and assistance (IAC, Electronic Business Center, PTRCs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Inventors Assistance Center (IAC) provides information on filing provisional and nonprovisional applications; the Electronic Business Center assists with EFS-Web; Public Search Facility and PTRCs provide search resources and assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent inventors can access webinars, brochures, search rooms, and local PTRCs; contact numbers and web resources are provided for help and to avoid scams/invention promoters.
